operationalization: Quantify within-species and left-right similarity for features that pass standard randomness tests, and compare that similarity with independent environmental noise. Excess bilateral or within-species agreement would reject ongoing environmental noise; agreement alone would not identify one intrinsic mechanism among other shared deterministic growth rules.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: public photographs of repeated and bilaterally symmetric organisms for pattern comparison

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimen media for comparing paired structures within individuals

obstacles: Shared genes or shared developmental history produce matching patterns without the specific intrinsic-randomness mechanism.
Which features count as complex and random has to be fixed before the similarity test is meaningful.
rationale: Image archives are sufficient to test the negative half, that fine-scale agreement is too strong for independent environmental noise, for some well-photographed organisms. They do not cover the stated range of physical and biological systems, and a positive match is also what any shared deterministic program would produce. The claim is therefore testable only in part and only against the environmental-noise rival.

operationalization: Compare a roughness or circularity statistic for random walks, Eden-like aggregation, and deterministic cellular automata against the same models with the randomness removed. The central-limit case is already a theorem; the aggregation and cellular-automaton cases are finite simulations. Continuity collapsing when randomness is removed, and matching when intrinsic randomness replaces external noise, would support the claim; a systematic counterexample in these classes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: published elementary and two-dimensional cellular-automaton evolutions, including rules that round under intrinsic randomness

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open environment for rerunning random walks, aggregation, and cellular automata

obstacles: Smoothness needs an explicit statistic; visual roundness alone is not a decision criterion.
The Eden model still lacks a full proof, so that case is settled by simulation rather than by theorem.
rationale: The claim is pinned to three reproducible model classes, not to an open-ended survey of nature. Random-walk distributions are covered by the central limit theorem, and the aggregation and cellular-automaton comparisons are short simulations in public software. Removing randomness, or swapping its source, is a direct control, so the stated comparison can be confirmed or refuted now.

operationalization: In ensembles of discrete growth and coarsening models, vary the ratio of the small-scale mixing time to the large-scale growth time and measure a continuity statistic of the large-scale interface. A sharp loss of continuity below a modest timescale separation would support the proposed necessary condition inside those ensembles; continuity without that separation would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: reference cellular-automaton rules for growth and domain coarsening

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for sweeping noise rate against growth rate

obstacles: The universal quantifier over every discrete system is not settled by any finite ensemble.
Continuous, slow, and random each need a definition before the threshold is meaningful.
rationale: The timescale comparison is a well-posed simulation inside the growth and coarsening models named in the section. A sample can refute a claimed necessary condition, but it cannot establish the condition for every discrete system. Coverage of the full general principle is therefore only partial.

operationalization: For one- and two-dimensional cellular automata drawn from stated rule classes, sweep the initial density of black cells and record whether the long-time density jumps from one absorbing color to the other near one half. The frequency of that jump, and of stuck domain walls, can then be compared across dimension. A rising frequency with dimension would support the claim; a flat or falling frequency would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of one-dimensional rules, including rule 184, against which the density sweep can be checked

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for density sweeps in one and two dimensions

obstacles: Fairly rare and increasingly common become numbers only after the rule ensemble is fixed.
Two- and higher-dimensional rule spaces must be sampled rather than exhaustively listed.
rationale: The decision criterion is a discrete change in the absorbing state as initial density crosses one half, which is unambiguous for a finite lattice. Elementary one-dimensional rules can be enumerated completely, and a stratified sample of two-dimensional rules is a standard computation of days to weeks. That is enough to confirm or refute the stated dimensional comparison.

operationalization: Count stable steady states and hysteresis in published chemical-kinetic and phase-transition systems as a continuous parameter is varied. Multiple stable states with an abrupt switch would support the dynamical half; a single stable branch throughout would count against it. Whether a discrete model is the most appropriate description is a separate modeling judgment and is not fixed by that count.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemical Kinetics Database
candidate_datasets.role: evaluated rate data for chemical reactions whose steady states can be checked for bistability

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook fluid properties
candidate_datasets.role: reference phase-equilibrium data for discrete liquid-vapor transitions under continuous temperature change

obstacles: Most appropriate is a normative choice among models, not a measured variable.
Kinetic compilations cover laboratory reactions, not every natural system with discrete behavior.
rationale: Bistability and first-order transitions in continuous equations are standard and are documented in public kinetic and thermodynamic compilations. The further claim that discrete models are therefore often the most appropriate has no agreed confirming measurement: continuous models remain adequate for many of the same transitions. Existing data test the dynamical half and not the modeling recommendation.

operationalization: For a pre-registered list of complex natural patterns, compare held-out predictive error of an explicit growth or evolution model with that of a constraint-satisfaction model, and separately measure how close random or locally improved configurations come to meeting the constraint. A large predictive gap in favor of explicit dynamics, together with search that stalls far from solutions, would support the claim on that list; the reverse would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: SAT Competition benchmarks
candidate_datasets.role: public discrete constraint instances and solver results for the computational-difficulty premise

obstacles: Best explained is not fixed by predictive error alone, so rival explanations can be redrawn after the fact.
There is no census of complex natural behavior on which almost none could be counted.
rationale: The computational premise, that exact satisfaction of hard discrete constraints is not reached by casual search, can be checked on public benchmark instances. The natural-history quantifier has no dataset that enumerates phenomena and their best explanations, and predictive comparisons exist only for scattered case studies. The claim can be probed for particular systems and not as a statement about almost all complex behavior.

operationalization: On a broad sample of discrete constraint problems, run strict downhill search, neutral-or-downhill search, and standard accelerated heuristics, and record residual violation and time to a solution. Near-universal trapping of downhill search, with only slow gains from added randomness and no heuristic that succeeds across the sample, would support the computational half; a general method that reliably reaches solutions would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SAT Competition benchmarks
candidate_datasets.role: public satisfiability instances and published solver outcomes for local and global search

obstacles: No speed-up works across broad classes is a negative existential and cannot be exhausted by the heuristics tried.
The inference from solver behavior to natural systems adds a step the benchmarks do not contain.
rationale: Jagged landscapes and trapping of downhill search are directly measurable on public constraint benchmarks, and those experiments are routine. A claim that no acceleration works across broad classes cannot be closed by any finite comparison, and the step from that fact to natural systems is an analogy rather than a dataset. The computational core is testable; the full conclusion is not settled by it.

operationalization: Compare measured packing fractions of identical disks under lateral compression, and of identical spheres under compression or vibration, with the proved maxima (hexagonal packing in two dimensions, about 0.74 in three). Disks reaching the hexagonal fraction, and spheres remaining well below the three-dimensional maximum under ordinary pushing and jiggling, would support the claim; spheres that routinely crystallize into the densest packing under those protocols would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Hales, A proof of the Kepler conjecture
candidate_datasets.role: published proof of the densest repetitive packing of equal spheres, the arrangement agitation is claimed to miss

obstacles: Outcome depends on the agitation protocol: shearing and slow annealing can crystallize spheres that gentle jiggling leaves jammed.
Experimental packing fractions are scattered across papers rather than held in one open campaign.
rationale: The target densities are mathematical and the two-dimensional case is classical, so the comparison itself is sharp. Laboratory results on random close packing are public but dispersed, and they show both jamming under simple agitation and crystallization under more careful driving. The claim is therefore decidable for specified protocols and not as an unqualified never across every way of jiggling.

operationalization: Classify biological forms by a pre-registered complexity measure and ask whether the developmental mechanism is a measured growth process or an optimality condition, using known gene-regulatory and morphogenetic data. Complex forms whose construction is a described growth program, and simple forms that match a constraint, would support the split; complex forms that are reached as optima without a growth program would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: genetic and developmental records for separating growth mechanisms from optimality stories in a model animal

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI
candidate_datasets.role: public genomes and literature links for developmental genes across taxa

obstacles: Simple and complex are not stable categories, and many forms can be described both as growth and as satisfying a constraint.
Developmental mechanisms are known in depth for few organisms.
rationale: Model-organism genetics can show that particular complex structures are built by explicit developmental programs, which tests the claim on a restricted set of forms. It does not decide that selection produces constraint-satisfying forms only when they are simple, because both descriptions can be fitted to the same outcome. The scope across biological forms is far wider than the cases with a known mechanism.

operationalization: Enumerate small cellular-automaton rule spaces, measure rule-table complexity against a behavioral-complexity statistic such as spacetime compressibility or Wolfram class, and compare rules that differ by one table entry. A weak or absent correlation, with adjacent rules in different classes, would support the claim; a tight monotone relation between rule complexity and behavioral complexity would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: complete published survey of elementary cellular automata for the rule-versus-behavior comparison

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for recomputing behavior of neighboring rules

obstacles: Behavioral complexity has several inequivalent measures, though the qualitative mismatch is stable across the usual ones.
rationale: The claim is a statement about simple programs, and the elementary cellular automata are a finite public object. Recomputing the Gray-code sequence of neighboring rules and scoring their output takes days with standard tools. A direct correspondence would show up as a strong correlation; its absence is a decisive result for the stated scope.

operationalization: Assemble nested natural patterns with a recorded growth direction or a time series, and class each as successive splitting or as aggregation and merging. A majority in the building-up class would support the frequency claim inside that sample; a majority of splitting or branching origins would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: HydroSHEDS
candidate_datasets.role: global river networks, the tributary case of nesting built by merging

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of branched and nested organismal forms whose growth direction is sometimes known

obstacles: Many nested forms have no observation that distinguishes splitting from building up.
More common is undefined without a sampling frame over natural nested patterns.
rationale: River networks are a clear building-up case with public hydrography, and some organisms have a known branching development. Most nested forms in nature lack the time or mechanism data needed to assign an origin, so a frequency of more common cannot be estimated for the full scope. Existing resources test examples, not the global suspicion.

operationalization: Simulate rules 184 and 110 and a family of domain models whose boundaries annihilate on contact, including random-walk boundaries, and test whether the merger genealogy is a nested tributary tree. A nested merger tree across that family would support the claim; a broad class of independently growing, then merging, domains whose genealogy is not nested would refute the essentially any quantifier.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: published evolutions of rules 184 and 110 from random initial conditions

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for annihilating domains and random-walk boundaries

obstacles: Fairly independently has to be defined before the family of systems is closed.
Nesting in rule 110 is approximate once the localized structures are coarse-grained.
rationale: Annihilating and coalescing boundaries are a standard stochastic process, and the named cellular automata are small computations. The genealogy of mergers is a concrete object, so the nested-tree description can be confirmed or replaced by a counterexample inside the stated class. That is a computation, not a new observation of nature.

operationalization: The recommendation that visual comparison is the best first assessment of a complex model does not name a measured variable or a result that would confirm or refute it independently of a prior judgment about what counts as an adequate test.
obstacles: Best and adequately assessed are methodological judgments, not outcomes that distinguish the recommendation from rival standards of model testing.
rationale: The claim is a prescription for scientific practice. Any later success or failure of a model can be reconciled with having looked at pictures first or at numbers first, because the claim does not fix what the pictures or the numbers must predict. No public dataset supplies a decision criterion that would settle it.

operationalization: Run the hexagonal exactly-one-neighbor cellular automaton and compare quantitative shape descriptors (branching order, facet-to-dendrite sequence, sixfold symmetry) with photographed snowflakes grown at known temperature and humidity. A match across the observed morphology diagram, better than rival growth models, would support the claim; systematic misses, especially the absence of temperature dependence, would refute it as an account of the main features.

candidate_datasets.name: SnowCrystals.com
candidate_datasets.role: public gallery and morphology notes for real snow crystals under recorded growth conditions

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for the hexagonal exactly-one-neighbor growth rule

obstacles: Visual resemblance is shared by several dendritic models and does not by itself identify latent-heat inhibition.
The rule has no temperature or humidity parameter, while real snowflake habit is controlled by both.
rationale: Public snowflake images and a one-page simulation are enough to test whether this specific rule reproduces measured habit classes. The rule's lack of dependence on the conditions that organize the Nakaya diagram is a discriminator, not merely a difference of taste. Even so, several continuum and lattice models produce similar dendrites, so a picture match would not establish this cellular automaton as the mechanism.

operationalization: Score time-lapse records of individual snowflakes for switches between branched and faceted outline as growth proceeds. Repeated alternation within single crystals would support the prediction; steady habit, or switches that track only external temperature changes, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SnowCrystals.com
candidate_datasets.role: laboratory photographs and growth descriptions of individual snow crystals, including some time development

obstacles: Most public images are finished crystals, so the time order of tree-like and faceted stages is often missing.
External changes in humidity can mimic an intrinsic growth-and-collision cycle.
rationale: The prediction is a specific time order, which is sharper than a static resemblance. Laboratory growth records exist but are scattered and rarely cover a full crystal from seed to completion under constant conditions. Those records can test the prediction for some habits and not for snowflake growth in general.

operationalization: Repeat crystal-growth runs from simple seeds in a controlled environment and compare the irregular outline across runs. Outlines that recur in detail would favor intrinsic generation by the growth rule; outlines that change with run, seed noise, or uncontrolled environment would favor external randomness.

candidate_datasets.name: SnowCrystals.com
candidate_datasets.role: controlled ice-crystal growth images, a restricted case of crystalline shape

obstacles: Repeat-run shape archives are rare outside a few laboratory systems such as ice and electrodeposits.
A deterministic model that looks irregular does not show that real crystals use that mechanism.
rationale: The discriminating observation is run-to-run repeatability under fixed conditions, not a simulation that looks rough. That observation exists for a few crystalline systems and is missing for most materials, so often across crystal shapes cannot be read off current public collections. The claim is testable on a restricted scope.

operationalization: Compare roughness statistics of fracture surfaces in single crystals, polycrystals, and mapped geological faults, and test whether a material-free displacement rule reproduces those statistics better than a model driven by pre-existing flaws. Equally rough single-crystal fractures, with the same exponents as faults, would support a material-independent mechanism; smooth cleavage, or roughness that tracks grain boundaries, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards
candidate_datasets.role: public earthquake and fault records for the geological end of the claimed range

obstacles: Single-crystal cleavage is often smooth on favored planes, so the sample of breaks is biased toward rough ones.
Matching a cellular-automaton picture does not show that the same mechanism operates from silicon to faults.
rationale: Fracture-roughness exponents and the contrast between cleavage and intergranular failure are published and partly public, and fault catalogs cover the large-scale end. Those data can reject a claim of universal roughness independent of material. They do not identify one deterministic cellular-automaton mechanism as the common cause across that range.

operationalization: Derive or simulate the large-scale momentum equation for particle or lattice-gas rules that conserve mass and momentum, and compare the resulting flow, at matched Reynolds number, with laboratory or direct numerical solutions of ordinary fluids. Universal Navier-Stokes behavior when the conservation laws and a randomness condition hold, and a different large-scale law when they are broken, would support the claim; a conserved, sufficiently random particle system whose large-scale flow is not hydrodynamic would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
candidate_datasets.role: public direct numerical simulations of incompressible flow for comparison with lattice-gas output

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook fluid properties
candidate_datasets.role: reference properties of ordinary fluids whose large-scale flow collapses under the same dimensionless laws

obstacles: The hydrodynamic limit assumes enough randomness and isotropy; some conserving rules stay correlated and do not yield simple viscosity.
Complex fluids are outside the ordinary fluids the claim is aimed at.
rationale: Mass and momentum conservation plus molecular chaos is the standard route to the Navier-Stokes equations, and lattice-gas rules can be rerun and compared with public turbulence fields. Breaking a conservation law changes the large-scale equation, which is a clean control. For ordinary fluids the claim can be confirmed or refuted with existing theory and data.

operationalization: Perturb public velocity fields at small scales and measure the growth or decay of the difference in large-scale observables such as wake spectra and coherent-structure positions. Rapid damping in almost every flow class would support the claim; exponential growth of large-scale differences in typical turbulent flows would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
candidate_datasets.role: public Navier-Stokes time series on which large-scale perturbation growth can be measured

obstacles: Large-scale and discernible depend on the filter, and predictability time varies by orders of magnitude across flows.
Almost all cases is not represented by the canonical simulations in one database.
rationale: Sensitive dependence of filtered fluid observables is a standard analysis, and public direct numerical simulations contain the fields. Those simulations can refute the claim for the flows they include if large-scale differences grow. They do not inventory almost all flows, and the cutoff between large-scale damping and chaos is itself a modeling choice, so the universal wording stays only partly testable.

operationalization: Compare deterministic Navier-Stokes simulations that contain no molecular noise with the same flows under added microscopic noise or altered inflow perturbations, and attribute the turbulent variance by scale. Turbulence that persists without molecular noise and without external forcing fluctuations would support intrinsic large-scale generation; turbulence that disappears when those sources are removed would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
candidate_datasets.role: deterministic high-resolution turbulent flows with no explicit molecular noise

obstacles: Laboratory inflows and boundaries always inject disturbances, so an external contribution is hard to set to zero.
Mostly is a partition of variance that different decompositions assign differently.
rationale: Deterministic simulations already produce turbulence, which bears directly on the claim that molecular noise is not required. Separating that intrinsic cascade from disturbances that entered through the boundaries is much harder in experiments, and public databases are single realizations of a few geometries. The claim is testable for those flows and not as a statement about turbulent fluids in general.

operationalization: Repeat a carefully prepared flow and compute the cross-run correlation of the velocity field in a regime whose single-run statistics pass randomness tests. High correlation despite random-looking statistics would support the prediction; correlation that collapses as soon as the flow looks random would refute it.
obstacles: Published repeatable flows are mostly regular vortex wakes, not flows that pass randomness tests.
Matched initial conditions at turbulent Reynolds numbers are rarely archived as an open dataset.
rationale: The prediction has a clear statistic: repeatability conditional on looking random. Experiments on a few vortices show repeatable intricate flow, which covers a weaker regime than the one claimed. Open archives of matched turbulent repeats that still look random are not available, so the prediction as stated is only partly tested.

operationalization: Run iterative random search for a fixed budget of about 10^12 evaluations on constraint landscapes graded by complexity, and compare the residual to the optimum. Rapid success only on simple landscapes would support the computational half. Calling organismal traits good enough rather than optimal further requires a measured fitness landscape, which this budget alone does not supply.

candidate_datasets.name: SAT Competition benchmarks
candidate_datasets.role: public hard constraint instances used to measure how far iterative search remains from a solution

obstacles: Significant complexity and good enough are not defined for real organisms.
Biological search is not a uniform random walk: recombination, population structure, and developmental bias change the effective budget.
rationale: Search cost on hard discrete constraints can be measured, and a trillion evaluations is a concrete budget for a simulation study of modest landscapes. Organismal fitness landscapes for complex traits are not a public dataset, so the conclusion that most features are merely good enough is not resolved by the computational analogy. The claim splits into a testable search statement and an unmeasured biological inference.

operationalization: Relate a complexity score of morphological traits to measures of selection and conservation, and compare the distribution of those traits with the distribution of outputs of short random programs. Complexity concentrated on weakly selected traits, and matching the random-program ensemble, would support the claim; complexity concentrated on strongly selected traits would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI
candidate_datasets.role: public genomes and sequence-conservation resources used as proxies for selection

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies for comparing trait change against relatedness

obstacles: A complex pattern can be both a side effect of a short program and maintained by selection.
Originates from is a historical cause, not a variable stored in sequence or trait databases.
rationale: Genomes and trees support a proxy comparison between morphological complexity and evidence of selection. That comparison does not isolate an abstract fact about random programs as the source of most biological complexity, because the same patterns are compatible with selection on coarse features. The causal claim is only weakly discriminated by existing data.

operationalization: Score a pre-registered complexity measure on comparable parts of organisms in fossil assemblages binned over the last several hundred million years. A flat trend after an early appearance would support the claim; a sustained rise or fall in that part-level measure would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: public fossil occurrences and taxonomic ranges through the Phanerozoic

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D and 2D media of specimens from which morphological complexity can be scored

obstacles: Soft textures and pigmentation rarely fossilize, so the record is biased toward hard parts.
Disparity of body plans is not the same variable as complexity of individual parts.
rationale: The fossil record can support a time series of morphological disparity, and public occurrence data cover much of the Phanerozoic for skeletonized taxa. They do not contain a measure of texture or part-level complexity of the kind the claim names, and preservation removes much of that signal. The claim is testable for some hard-part proxies and not for the stated features in general.

operationalization: Identify the gene-regulatory elements that control shell pigmentation and measure their functional length, then test whether that length is short relative to a pre-registered baseline. Within-species pattern variety is only a proxy: high variety together with a short mapped program would support the claim, while a long program would refute it even if patterns vary.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI
candidate_datasets.role: mollusc genome assemblies, which do not yet map the pigmentation programs whose length is at issue

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic backbone for shelled molluscs, without genetic program lengths

obstacles: Pattern variety can come from many polymorphic loci in a long program, so diversity does not measure length.
The pigmentation programs for shell patterns have not been isolated for a representative set of species.
rationale: Program length is a measurable quantity once the responsible regulatory program is identified, so the prediction is testable in principle. Public genomes and taxonomic catalogs do not contain those programs or their lengths, and the diversity proxy does not decide brevity. Resolving the claim requires data that have not been collected.

operationalization: Compare the response to selection, in breeding data or in evolutionary simulations, for traits graded from simple scalar properties to high-dimensional patterns. Systematic response confined to simple traits would support the claim; reliable optimization of complex patterns would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: genetic and phenotypic data for a model animal in which selection on simple and complex traits can be compared

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI
candidate_datasets.role: public sequences and linked phenotype resources across organisms

obstacles: Simple behavior and meaningful optimization are not operational without a chosen trait decomposition.
Artificial selection on complex quantitative traits often works, which pressures the wording but does not map cleanly onto the claim's notion of complexity.
rationale: Quantitative genetics can measure whether a chosen trait responds to selection, and that test exists for many simple traits and some complex ones. The claim's partition into quite simple and complex behavior is not a standard variable, so different decompositions give different answers. Existing data constrain examples and do not settle the general limitation.

operationalization: Measure modularity, independence of parts, and smoothness of trait variation for characters ranked by evidence of selection. A positive association between selection and those engineering-like properties would support the claim; complex, tightly coupled traits under strong selection would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: gene and phenotype data for testing whether selected traits are more modular

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI
candidate_datasets.role: comparative genomic data linked to organismal traits

obstacles: Like systems in engineering is a metaphor until modularity and smooth adjustability are defined.
Selection is often inferred from the same simplicity the claim treats as its effect.
rationale: Modularity and the smoothness of quantitative traits can be measured in model organisms, which gives a partial test. The main effect of selection is a global causal claim, and public datasets do not separate selection's effect from developmental constraints that produce simple parts for other reasons. Discriminating power stays low.

operationalization: Among species in a clade, estimate evolutionary rate for each trait and score trait complexity independently, then test whether the fastest traits are the most complex and the most conserved traits are those with independent evidence of selection. A positive rate-complexity relationship would support the claim; fast change in simple traits, or slow change in the most complex ones, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies of related species on which trait rates can be compared

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of pigmentation and structural traits across closely related species

obstacles: Inferring selection from constancy makes the second clause circular.
Complexity scored from photographs is observer-dependent, and quantitative matrices exist for few clades.
rationale: Phylogenies and image collections make a rate-versus-complexity comparison feasible for particular groups such as molluscs, fishes, or butterflies. Coverage is a subset of related species, and treating conservation as evidence of selection builds the conclusion into the measurement. The pattern can be tested where traits have been coded and not as a general biological rule.

operationalization: For structures that arose more than once, estimate how often short programs of the relevant class emit that structure, and compare functional performance with alternatives that do not recur. Recurrence of structures that are common in the program sample and not superior in performance would support the claim; recurrence only of structures that outperform alternatives would favor optimality.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies used to identify independent origins of similar structures

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of simple-program outputs for estimating which patterns are common

obstacles: Common in program space depends on the class of programs one samples.
Optimality and historical availability are both compatible with the same repeated structure.
rationale: Independent origins can be read from public phylogenies, and the frequency of a pattern among small programs can be counted. Those two measurements do not decide between a shared developmental attractor and selection for performance, because both predict recurrence. The claim is only partly discriminated, and only for structures that have been functionally compared.

operationalization: Track a complexity measure, such as number of distinct parts or a disparity statistic, across fossil lineages and test whether the maximum and the typical value rise inevitably, and whether decreases are common. A ceiling that does not rise in many long-lived lineages, together with frequent simplification, would support the negative claim about inevitability; a systematic increase confined to lineages under stronger selection would count against the proposed roles of mutation and selection.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences for trends in diversity and morphological range through time

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic context for separating lineage age from change in complexity

obstacles: The fossil record shows maximum complexity and typical complexity moving differently, so the trend depends on the statistic.
Random mutation versus selection is not identified by the direction of the trend alone.
rationale: Public fossil data can reject a claim that organisms inevitably become more elaborate, because many old lineages stay simple and some trends reverse. They do not show that increases come from nonfatal random mutations while selection's systematic effect is to simplify, since those causes are not variables in the occurrence record. The negative half is partly testable; the causal partition is not.

operationalization: Fit fixed-angle, fixed-length-ratio branching rules to measured plant architectures from algae through woody plants, and compare them with alternative growth rules on held-out geometry. A small family of substitution rules that recovers most branching topologies would support the claim; systematic residuals that require other mechanisms would refute it for those taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: compiled plant traits, including size and some architectural variables

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of branching form across plant groups

obstacles: Trait databases record size and leaves more often than full branching angles and length ratios.
A geometric fit does not show that the apex uses that substitution rule rather than auxin-mediated branching.
rationale: Branching geometry can be compared with substitution-system output, and public images and trait compilations cover many growth forms. The compilations are thin on the actual angles and length ratios, and a successful fit does not discriminate the developmental mechanism from other branching models. The claim is testable as a geometric description for a subset of plants.

operationalization: Generate leaf outlines from the same branching-parameter family used for whole-plant form, and compare them with measured leaf contours across smooth, toothed, and lobed species. Recovery of the outline range by small parameter changes would support the geometric half; outlines that stay outside that family, or developmental maps that build the margin by a different process, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: leaf-trait measurements across many species

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of leaf outlines for comparison with branching models

obstacles: Outline similarity is produced by several margin-growth models and does not identify the branching process.
Leaf shape is usually fixed inside the bud by marginal patterning, which is not the same measurement as a stem-substitution rule.
rationale: It is a short computation to show that small parameter changes in a branching rule swing the outline from smooth to prickly. Matching those outlines to real leaves can be attempted with public images and trait data, but resemblance is a weak test against other developmental models. Existing data do not establish that leaves and whole plants are produced by the same process.

operationalization: Measure divergence angles in a wide sample of plants and run the local-depletion model, testing whether it converges to about 137.5 degrees and whether physical or chemical inhibition experiments do the same without a fitness search. Convergence to that angle under inhibition, including in nonliving analogs, would support the growth mechanism; a different angle, or an angle that appears only when a shading optimum is imposed, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: plant-trait compilation; divergence angles themselves are sparse and must be supplemented from the botanical literature

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of phyllotactic spirals for a coarse check of pattern prevalence

obstacles: There is no single open archive of measured divergence angles across the plant kingdom.
Showing that a growth rule yields the angle does not by itself prove that selection played no role in retaining it.
rationale: The angle is a sharp prediction, and both the inhibition model and nonliving experiments that produce it are reproducible with public methods and published measurements. Those measurements are dispersed rather than deposited as one dataset, and photographs do not replace goniometry. The mechanism is testable now for well-studied plants; the further denial of any optimizing role for selection is not settled by the same evidence.

operationalization: Sample the few-parameter shell-growth model on a grid of expansion, translation, and aperture shape, and ask what fraction of occupied cells have a matching specimen. A match for essentially every cell would support the claim; a substantial region of the model with no real shell would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: digitized museum mollusc specimens and images spanning shell morphospace

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic inventory of living and extinct molluscs against which model forms can be checked

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of coiled shells for forms poorly represented in scanned collections

obstacles: Image coverage is uneven, so an empty cell in the model may be a gap in digitization.
Matching a geometric parameter to a shell is partly a judgment about which coiling features count.
rationale: The model is a small parameter sweep, and public specimen portals contain large numbers of shells across the classical morphospace. That is enough to test occupation of much of the model. It is not enough to certify that essentially every generated form occurs, because rare geometries and photographic gaps remain. The claim is resolvable in large part and not in full.

operationalization: Measure the spatial range of morphogen gradients and the order in which region-specific genes, including Hox genes, become distinct, and test whether subdivisions appear only after a region reaches a few tenths of a millimeter, with proximal regions before distal ones. That order across animals would support the claim; simultaneous specification, or a length scale that changes freely with embryo size, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: expression and genetic data for hierarchical patterning in Drosophila

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish gene-expression and phenotype data for vertebrate embryonic regions

obstacles: The length scale and the genetic cascade are well measured in model species and poorly measured in most phyla.
Necessarily is a theoretical inference; some lineages specify fate in ways that do not follow a single fixed length.
rationale: Gradient ranges, Hox expression, and proximal-before-distal differentiation are standard measurements in public model-organism databases. Those data can confirm the hierarchical pattern for insects and vertebrates and can reveal exceptions. They do not cover animal embryos in general, so the claim of an almost inevitable hierarchy for animals is only partly resolved.

operationalization: Place landmarks on related species within a family or order and test whether the shape differences are smooth relative warps consistent with different regional growth rates. A low-dimensional smooth transformation relating the shapes would support the claim; discrete additions of parts that no smooth warp removes would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimen media for geometric morphometrics of related animals

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: museum specimen images spanning breeds and species within higher taxa

obstacles: Landmark datasets are dense for some vertebrate groups and absent for most animal orders.
A smooth geometric map can describe a difference that was not produced by altered growth rates.
rationale: Geometric morphometrics is a standard test of whether related forms differ by smooth transformations, and public specimen media cover several well-studied families. A successful warp does not establish relative growth rate as the cause, and many taxa have no landmark series. The claim is testable for shape description in a subset of animals.

operationalization: Show that small changes in simple growth rules change simulated form sharply, then ask whether real diversity is concentrated among traits whose genetic differences look like draws from a short random rule rather than like selected parameter tuning. A match between observed form diversity and the random-rule ensemble, without a selection signal, would support the claim; diversity that tracks measured functional optima would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: examples of how small rule changes alter pattern complexity

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: images of plant and animal form diversity for a coarse comparison

obstacles: Randomly picked is not observable from adult form.
Sensitivity of a model to its parameters does not show that evolution samples rules that way.
rationale: The computational phenomenon, that nearby simple rules diverge in form, is immediate to check. The biological claim that most diversity and complexity come from essentially random sampling of such rules is a historical cause that images and program catalogs do not record. Existing resources illustrate the mechanism and do not resolve its responsibility for most organismal form.

operationalization: Treat each shell pattern as a space-time record and test whether a symmetrical nearest-neighbor two-color rule reproduces it, then compare the set of successful rules with the set of patterns on real shells. A close match of the two ranges would support the claim; many common shell patterns that require longer-range or multi-state rules, or a physiological map that is not a local neighbor rule, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic index of patterned molluscs whose shells can be targeted for images

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: museum images of shell pigmentation usable as space-time records

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: the elementary symmetric cellular-automaton patterns used as the comparison class

obstacles: A similar range of pictures can be produced by reaction-diffusion models that are not cellular automata.
The pigment physiology of the mantle edge is rarely measured, so rule inference from the shell is a proxy for the mechanism.
rationale: Because the shell stores successive rows, local determinism can be tested by rule inference rather than by a glance at resemblance. Public images and the finite list of symmetric elementary rules make that comparison feasible for a substantial sample. Physiology that would confirm neighbor-to-neighbor secretion is mostly missing, so the mechanism remains less resolved than the geometric range.

operationalization: Compare the distribution of pattern complexity between species whose shells stay covered by an opaque layer and species whose patterns are visible, against the distribution of the simplest cellular-automaton rules. Similar complexity in permanently hidden patterns would weaken optimization for visibility; a restriction of complex patterns to visible shells would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic list of molluscs that can be joined to descriptions of periostracum and pattern

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs showing whether a pattern is exposed or covered in life

obstacles: Opacity and pattern are recorded in scattered descriptions, not in one coded dataset.
A hidden pattern could still be a side effect of selection on a linked visible or structural trait.
rationale: Permanently covered patterns are a natural comparison that existing photographs and taxonomic descriptions can support for many species. The comparison is informative against selection for being seen, and it is silent about other functions. Compiling opacity and complexity across molluscs is a real curation task, so the test is partial rather than immediate.

operationalization: Simulate the local-activation, longer-range-inhibition rule across a grid of distance weights and compare the resulting spots, labyrinths, and stripes with measured animal patterns, including experimental shifts in wavelength when the inhibitor is perturbed. A match of pattern class and of the experimental wavelength shift would support the mechanism family; patterns or perturbations outside that family would count against this rule.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish pigment-pattern genetics and images, the best-studied experimental case

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of spots, stripes, and labyrinths across animals

obstacles: Many reaction-diffusion and cell-movement models produce the same three pattern classes.
The specific cellular-automaton weights are not identifiable from adult coat photographs.
rationale: Public images show that a few pattern classes recur, and zebrafish experiments test local activation and longer-range inhibition directly. Those experiments support the mechanism family and do not single out one weighted cellular-automaton rule among many models with the same interaction. The claim is partly resolved at the level of the interaction and not at the level of the exact rule.

operationalization: Decompose short-horizon price variance into intervals with identified external news and intervals without it, at timescales of seconds to minutes. Variance that remains large in no-news windows, and that is shared across unrelated instruments traded on the same venue, would support an internal source; variance that collapses to the news timestamps would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Binance public market data
candidate_datasets.role: downloadable tick-level trade data for a large public market

obstacles: Unobserved information can move prices in windows that contain no headline.
Freely archived tick data are dominated by crypto, while equity tick histories are often licensed.
rationale: Second- and minute-scale trades are public for at least one major class of market, and an event-style split between news and no-news windows is a standard analysis. That split can show that a large fraction of short-term variance is not tied to public headlines. It cannot fully separate internal matching dynamics from private information, so the mechanism remains only partly identified.

operationalization: Enumerate one-dimensional two-color rules, mark those for which a local perturbation eventually reaches every site, and test the running difference of black and white counts for compressibility and standard randomness statistics. Random running totals confined to the propagating rules would support the claim; propagating rules whose running totals stay simple, or non-propagating rules whose totals look random, would refute the stated link.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: published elementary rules used to separate propagating from non-propagating behavior

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for the buy-minus-sell running total of each rule

obstacles: Statistical tests can fail to find regularity without proving that the total is random.
Eventually propagate has to be judged on a finite lattice and a finite time horizon.
rationale: The claim is about a finite family of cellular automata, with an explicit control: rules that spread information versus rules that do not. Both the classification and the randomness statistics of the running total are routine computations. A counterexample in that family would refute the inevitability claim, and none requires new market data.

operationalization: As stated, the claim asserts only that there may be some very simple program from which known physics emerges. No particular program, observable, or contradicting outcome is specified, so no measurement confirms or refutes it.
obstacles: A hedged existence claim is compatible both with every current observation and with the failure to exhibit such a program.
Matching a simple program to all of known physics would require a specific candidate that the claim does not provide.
rationale: The wording is modal: there could be a simple underlying program. Until a definite program is proposed, every dataset is consistent with the claim and with its denial. Similar-looking simulations would not test it, and no public resource distinguishes this hypothesis from rival foundations.

operationalization: Decide reversibility for each of the 256 two-color nearest-neighbor rules and for each of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules, using a fixed injectivity test, and count the reversible cases. Exactly six and exactly 1800 would confirm the claim; any other counts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: published elementary cellular automata, enough to recheck the two-color count of six

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for inspecting candidate reversible rules after they are enumerated

obstacles: Reversibility on the infinite line, on periodic lattices, and on finite strings need not coincide, so the predicate must match the one used for the count of 1800.
The three-color space is trillions of rules; the test is finite but large.
rationale: Both numbers are exact claims about finite, fully specified rule spaces. The two-color count is a few seconds of computation, and the three-color count is a known decision procedure applied to a large but finite set, feasible for a small team with a cluster in weeks rather than a missing dataset. A discrepancy in either count would refute the claim.

operationalization: Construct second-order reversible cellular automata and compare them with irreversible rules on compressibility of the spacetime pattern and on the presence of persistent localized structures. Reversible examples that are incompressible and that support localized structures would support the claim; reversible rules that remain simple under every standard construction would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: reference irreversible cellular automata and published reversible constructions

candidate_datasets.name: NetLogo
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for second-order reversible rules and localized structures

obstacles: As complex as anywhere else depends on the complexity measure, although incompressible output and localized structures are directly checkable.
rationale: The claim is an existence claim about a class of programs that can be built by a standard reversible construction. Generating apparent randomness and localized structures in that class is a short computation, and failure to find either under a broad sample of constructions would count against it. No new empirical data are required.

operationalization: For reversible cellular automata and for laboratory thermodynamic systems, compare entropy change from simple prepared initial conditions with the computational cost of finding initial conditions that decrease randomness. Entropy increase from every simple preparation, and no shorter search for decreasing preparations than running the dynamics, would support the account for those systems; an easy construction of randomness-decreasing states, or simple preparations whose entropy falls, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: reversible cellular-automaton examples on which entropy from simple initial conditions can be recomputed

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook fluid properties
candidate_datasets.role: reference thermodynamic properties of ordinary fluids, the systems where entropy increase is best documented

obstacles: A cosmological low-entropy initial condition predicts the same laboratory facts without the computational story.
The claim that no shorter procedure exists is a general complexity statement, not a quantity tabulated for physical experiments.
rationale: Entropy increase from simple initial conditions can be recomputed for reversible cellular automata and is extensively documented for gases. The explanation that this happens because finding atypical initial conditions is as hard as the evolution itself is not distinguished, by those data, from other typicality arguments. The empirical regularity is partly testable; the stated cause is not settled by existing resources.
